# Installation and setup instructions

The chapters of this book focused on population genomics and simulations rely
pretty much exclusively on the R package
[_slendr_](https://bodkan.github.io/slendr), plus an assortment of other useful
R packages for data science (most of which will be automatically installed
alongside _slendr_). Below are instructions how to prepare everything that will
be needed before the start of our workshop.

**Please don't hesitate to get in touch with me over email at `contact [snail
sign] bodkan.net` if you run into any problems with this setup procedure or
anything else related to this! If you're reading this in preparation for one of
my in-person workshops, you can also catch me whenever you see me at the
teaching venue.**

## Installation steps

1. **I assume you already have [R](https://www.r-project.org) and
[RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) installed on your
computer (any reasonably recent version will do).**

2. **Open RStudio and copy this into the R console to install the _slendr_
package:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("slendr")
```

**Note:** If you get an error during the installation, please copy-and-paste
the entire output from this command and send it to me via email.

3. **Paste this little testing simulation script into the R console to make
sure that everything works correctly.** Don't read too much into the meaning of
the code, understanding (and being able to program) all this and much, much
more will be the point of our workshop.

```{r}
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)

init_env(uv = TRUE)

A <- population("popA", time = 8000, N = 1000)
B <- population("popB", time = 4000, N = 1000, parent = A)
C <- population("popC", time = 4000, N = 1000, parent = A)
D <- population("popD", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = C)

gf <- list(
  gene_flow(from = B, to = D, start = 1000, end = 800, proportion = 0.2),
  gene_flow(from = C, to = D, start = 1000, end = 800, proportion = 0.1)
)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(A, B, C, D),
  gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 30
)

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)
ts
```

The outcome of this script should approximately match what you see above (minus
some statistical noise manifesting in your numbers in the summary being
slightly different).

4. **Installing a couple of bonus R packages**

In order to be able to run my solutions to some of the exercises (particularly
some more advanced optional bonus exercises), a couple of additional R packages
might be useful. Feel free to only install those if you run into them at a
later point.

You can install those packages with this command:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("combinat", "cowplot", "smartsnp", "viridis", "ggrepel", "cowplot", "forcats", "readr"))
```

---

**If you've made it this far, you're good to go!**

## Optional

**The following isn't something you need to do before the start of the
workshop. It's something we can deal with towards the end of the workshop (if
it even becomes necessary).

### Running heavy _slendr_ simulations

If you decide you'd like to run some really big simulations (perhaps during the
open-ended sessions at the end of the workshop) it might be necessary to run
your models on a bigger computing server. I suspect you have some remote
computing facilities available for doing heavy bioinformatics work, etc.

If that's the case, you'll want to also install and setup _slendr_ and the R
packages mentioned above on this remote server as well. Just repeat the same
instructions and you should be good to go.

### Running third-party software

Similarly, in the open-ended workshop sessions, you will have the opportunity
to apply the modeling techniques learned throughout the exercises in a
practical context of your own research. As you work on the exercises, you might
get an inspiration for applying this or that technique to study a particular
aspect of your research question, which might involve third-party software such
as qpAdm, IBDSeq, DATES, ADMIXTURE/STRUCTURE etc. If that ends up being the
case, I suggest you try to install _slendr_ on the (probably remote?) computing
server you normally use to do your research.
